Create exactly three measurable learning objectives. Do not invent course assignments, policies, measurements, datasets, instruction encodings, or product behavior that is absent from the supplied excerpts. Sequence the beats from foundations through application and end with a practical analysis checklist. Use only the supplied source excerpts for factual claims. Topic: CSCI-571: Honors Capstone Research. This catalog entry has student-, instructor-, or term-specific content. Create a rigorous orientation companion that teaches the stable process, standards, planning methods, evaluation criteria, and representative examples without inventing a fixed RIT syllabus. Official catalog description: This course allows students to pursue two threads of research in computer science. One thread is the discovery and analysis of previous work in the field. Students will select, read and collectively discuss papers from conferences and journals in CS. A survey paper on a topic of the student's choice will be required. The other thread is an independent project. Students will select a topic, lay out weekly goals, and meet with the instructor weekly. A final report and presentation will be required. Enrollment in this course requires permission from the department offering the course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring

Source excerpts:

[acm-code-of-ethics]
The ACM Code directs computing professionals to contribute to society and human well-being. Computing professionals should avoid harm. They should be honest and trustworthy. They should be fair and take action not to discriminate. They should respect the work required to produce new ideas and creative works. They should respect privacy. They should honor confidentiality. Professionals should strive to achieve high quality in both processes and products. They should maintain high standards of professional competence, conduct, and ethical practice. Robust security should be designed and implemented when appropriate. Ethical computing decisions identify stakeholders, foreseeable benefits and harms, uncertainty, alternatives, and obligations.

[acm-research-practice]
Responsible technical communication distinguishes claims from evidence. It cites prior work and identifies the contribution being reported. Methods should be described well enough for readers to evaluate the work. Results should be reported accurately rather than selected to create a misleading conclusion. Limitations and threats to validity should be made visible. Authors should preserve research integrity and avoid plagiarism, fabrication, and falsification. Conflicts and relevant relationships should be disclosed according to publication policy. A research project narrows a question, reviews literature, defines a reproducible method, evaluates results, and communicates for the intended audience.

[rit-csci-571]
This course allows students to pursue two threads of research in computer science. One thread is the discovery and analysis of previous work in the field. Students will select, read and collectively discuss papers from conferences and journals in CS. A survey paper on a topic of the student's choice will be required. The other thread is an independent project. Students will select a topic, lay out weekly goals, and meet with the instructor weekly. A final report and presentation will be required. Enrollment in this course requires permission from the department offering the course. Contact Hours: Lecture 3 Typically Offered: Fall, Spring
